opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I've been in this field for a long time, more than forty years now, so I've lived through quite a few of these waves. I remember the excitement in the early eighties about expert systems and industrial robots. People were sure factories would be fully automated within a decade. Then came the AI winter, and the funding dried up, and a lot of people left the field.

So when I see the current enthusiasm, especially around humanoid robots and the idea that the large language model breakthroughs will carry straight over into the physical world, I have mixed feelings. Part of me is thrilled. There's real progress, a lot of talented young people are coming into robotics, and there's investment we never dreamed of. But part of me worries, because I've seen what happens when expectations get way ahead of reality. When the hype doesn't pan out, there's a backlash, and that can set the whole field back by years.

The thing people often don't appreciate is what's sometimes called Moravec's paradox: the things that are easy for humans, like picking up a cup or folding a towel, are incredibly hard for robots, while the things we find hard, like chess or calculus, turned out to be comparatively easy for computers. Language models had the internet, trillions of words of training data. We don't have anything comparable for robot manipulation. There's no internet of robot motions. I've called it the 100,000-year data gap, roughly how long it would take to gather as much robot data as there is text used to train these models.

So my message is usually: be excited, but be patient. I think robots will get steadily better, and good old-fashioned engineering combined with learning will get us there. But it'll be incremental, not a sudden revolution where humanoids are doing your laundry next year. And I think being honest about that actually protects the field. It keeps the trust and the funding going over the long haul.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current enthusiasm has brought investment into robotics and warns that backlash can set the field back and disrupt funding, identifying excitement as a source of research resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've been in this field a long time, so I've lived through several of these waves now, and I have mixed feelings about them. On one hand, the excitement is wonderful. It brings in talent, it brings in funding, it gets young people interested in robotics, and that's genuinely good for the field. On the other hand, I worry about what happens when the hype gets ahead of the reality.

I've started calling this a "hype bubble." If you remember around 2015, 2016, there were very confident predictions that we'd have fully self-driving cars everywhere by 2020, that truck drivers would be out of work within a few years. That didn't happen. And when expectations get inflated like that, there's a correction. People get disillusioned, funding dries up, and the field goes through what we've historically called an "AI winter." I lived through one of those, and it's not pleasant.

So right now, with the large language models and all the talk about humanoid robots doing everything a person can do, I feel a certain déjà vu. I think the progress in AI is real and remarkable. But robotics is a different problem. There's this thing I often point to, Moravec's paradox: the things that are easy for humans, like picking up a cup or folding laundry, turn out to be extremely hard for robots, while things that are hard for humans, like playing chess, are comparatively easy for machines. We've known that for decades, and it's still true.

The core issue is that robots have to deal with the physical world, and the physical world is messy. There's uncertainty in sensing, uncertainty in control, uncertainty in the physics itself. When I move my hand to grasp something, I don't know exactly where the object is, I don't know exactly where my fingers will end up, and friction behaves in ways that are really hard to model. Language models don't face that. They operate in a clean symbolic space with essentially infinite training data scraped from the internet. We don't have the equivalent of the internet for robot manipulation. Nobody's been recording billions of hours of robots successfully picking things up.

So my view is that we should temper the excitement, not kill it. I'd love for the predictions to come true. I'd love to have a robot in my home that could clean up the kitchen. But I think we're talking about decades, not years, for general-purpose capability, and I think it's healthier for the field if we're honest about that. Otherwise we set ourselves up for another crash.

r001.rationale: The response says excitement brings talent and funding and gets young people interested in robotics, describing these as good for the field.

astra-6.text:
I’m excited, but I’m also cautious. In AI and robotics, we have these cycles where something works spectacularly well, and then we extrapolate: if it can do this, surely it’ll soon be able to do everything else. But those next steps can be much harder than they look.

Robotics has a particularly unforgiving reality check: the physical world. A demonstration is one thing; getting a robot to perform reliably across all the variations it encounters is another. Objects move, lighting changes, things wear out.

That doesn’t diminish the progress. There’s a lot to be excited about. I just think the most productive question is less ‘When will robots do everything?’ and more ‘Where can these systems be useful, and how can they work effectively with people?’

r001.rationale: The response describes recurring excitement cycles and cautions against overextrapolating, but does not say those waves provide resources for AI or robotics research.

sol-6.1.text:
I have a mixture of excitement and skepticism. There are real advances, and it’s wonderful to see people getting interested in these problems. But excitement tends to run ahead of what the systems can reliably do, particularly in robotics. You can show a robot doing something impressive once, and that’s very different from having it work consistently in an ordinary home or workplace.

So I try to ask: under what conditions does it work? How often does it fail? And what happens when it encounters something unexpected? Those questions can sound a little deflating, but they’re where a lot of the interesting research begins. I’m optimistic about the progress; I’m more cautious about the timelines.

r001.rationale: The response says excitement gets people interested and that questions spur research, but it does not identify excitement waves as a source of research resources.
